Back in the trees the tread improves up to a cabin at about 3,600 ft, sited just after a creek crossing — bunks, a wood stove and a logbook, and a useful emergency shelter. About a quarter mile past it, cross the creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

The lower part of this corridor is national recreation area and needs a park backcountry permit for camping; above the boundary it is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There is no rock start to find on this route. What you are finding is the right GULLY out of a basin that offers several, and getting that wrong is how parties get cliffed out.

Above where the tread dies, climb the Freezeout drainage and work up steep heather, talus and scree toward the NOTCH ON THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT. That notch is the target and it is the only feature in the upper basin worth navigating to. Cross to the east side of the creek at roughly 5,000 ft on the way up.

THE PHYSICAL TESTS ON THE CLIMB ITSELF ARE ROCK QUALITY AND TERRAIN GRADE, in that order. This is granite and the rock is genuinely good — clean, coarse and solid, the sort people compare to the best cragging ranges. It is mostly class 2 with short class 3 steps, and the crux is a steeper band with KRUMMHOLZ AND BLUFFS where you are pulling on vegetation-covered rock. If you are roping up, you are off route.

THE NEGATIVE MARKER IS ENORMOUS AND UNMISTAKABLE. This peak's north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs holding ice or the remains of it, with a glacier at its foot. If you are looking up at that, you are on the wrong side of the mountain entirely and you are under the technical routes. The scramble never sees the north face.

MARK YOUR EXACT ASCENT GULLY BEFORE YOU LEAVE IT, and this is the single most important sentence here. The upper basin holds several gullies and chutes that look alike from above, and dropping into the wrong one on descent risks cliffing out on bluffs well above the creek. Do not improvise a shortcut down. Reverse exactly what you came up.

Near the summit, watch teetering blocks, and expect the final ground to be exposed and windy.
hazards: Several similar-looking gullies in the upper basin; the wrong one cliffs out above the creek
The steep rock-and-alder section above the trail junction is the hardest navigation of the approach
Krummholz and vegetation-covered rock on the crux band
Teetering blocks near the summit
Days long enough that parties routinely finish the descent in the dark, with a boat pickup to make

approach_variants.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass
approach_variants.season: Late July through September, once the high road is open and the traverse is clear of snow
approach_variants.notes:
The third way in, and the one that trades a boat for a great deal of walking. The high pass road climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. It opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July, and closes with the first serious autumn storms.

From the pass, the crest trail runs north through country that starts near 6,200 ft and barely drops below 5,000 ft, over a high pass and on to Castle Pass, where it meets the Boundary Trail running east across the Pasayten and west toward the lake. Camps along the way are open and windy; pitch behind timber rather than in the meadow.

This stays inside the United States throughout, and it needs no boat.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Castle Pass the peak is immediately to the north-east, and what you are looking for is the head of the drainage on its southern flank rather than a base of rock.

Drop off the pass into the head of the creek basin on the peak's south side and work up it. The scramble ground is the same ground the eastern approach reaches from the other direction: heather, talus and scree leading to the NOTCH ON THE RIDGE AT ABOUT 7,600 FT, then class 2 granite with short class 3 steps to the summit.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THE ROCK. Once you are on it, the granite is clean, coarse and solid, and the difficulty stays at scrambling grade with one steeper krummholz-and-bluff band as the crux. Roped climbing means you are not on the standard route.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is the whole mountain: the north side is a fourteen-hundred-foot granite wall above a glacier. From anywhere on this approach you should be looking at broken scrambling ground, not at a wall. If a wall is above you, you have gone round the mountain.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is a legal one rather than a navigational one. The summit sits about a mile south of the international boundary and the boundary clearing is visible from high on the peak. Do not follow ground north from the summit or from the basin. Crossing on foot away from a port of entry is not a lawful crossing, the corridor is patrolled, and this is the one mistake here that ends with more than a long walk.

On descent, mark your ascent gully. The basin holds several that look alike from above and the wrong one cliffs out.
hazards: A long unpaved mountain road with 17 percent grades, no passing room and an unguarded drop
The road opens late and closes with the first autumn storms
Very long approach on foot with exposed, windy high camps
The international boundary lies about a mile north of the summit and crossing it here is unlawful
Similar-looking descent gullies that cliff out above the creek

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_south_route._why: The row stores only the approach that crosses the international boundary cross-country, which its own access notes say is not a lawful crossing; the same basin is reachable from inside the United States and that needs saying.
_sources: Route row's own approach, beta and descent columns; independent area summary confirming the peak is reached from the provincial park to the north, the crest trail to the west, or Freezeout Creek to the east, and that the wholly-US option is the slow one

approach_variants.name: The crest trail north from Harts Pass to Castle Pass, then the head of Castle Creek
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September, once the basin brush and wetlands are passable and the high road is open
approach_variants.notes:
READ THIS FIRST. The line most often written up for this route walks in from the provincial park to the north and crosses the international boundary cross-country in the clearing south of the creek. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over.

The way that stays inside the United States is the crest trail. The high pass road climbs about twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama, single track with pullouts rather than passing room, a wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades near seventeen percent high up. Trailers are prohibited. It opens with the snowmelt, usually early to mid July.

From the pass the crest trail runs north for a long way over high, open country to Castle Pass, where the Boundary Trail crosses. Castle Creek heads right there, so the pass puts you at the top of the basin this route climbs from.

The other wholly-US option is the eastern one — a boat across the lake and the abandoned creek trail — but that lands you on the far side of the mountain and serves the standard scramble rather than this line.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route works from a camp in the basin at about 5,500 ft, so the first thing to find is the basin floor rather than any rock. From the pass, drop into the head of the creek and follow it down and out into the open basin below the peak's south side. The lower ground here is alder, brush and wetland openings; the walking improves as you gain the basin proper.

FROM CAMP THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF TWO GULLIES AND A NOTCH, and each hands off to the next. First, the WIDE GULLY ON THE SOUTH SIDE — the broad one, not a narrow chute. Take it to roughly 6,800 ft. Second, at about that height, move INTO THE NORTH-EAST GULLY and aim for a NOTCH at around 7,400 ft. Third, from the notch, cross granite slabs, boulders and lingering snow patches south of the top, and finish with a short scramble to the true summit.

THE PHYSICAL TEST THROUGHOUT IS THAT NOTHING IS STEEP. Granite slabs, boulders and snow patches are the correct texture. If a rope comes out of the pack for anything other than a snow patch, you are not on this line.

NEGATIVE MARKER, and it is the whole north half of the mountain: the north face is a fourteen-hundred-foot wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier, carrying several hard routes. If that is above you, you have walked round the peak and you are under the technical climbing.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER, on the boundary. The summit sits about a mile south of the international line and the boundary clearing is a visible feature from up here. Do not use it as a route, and do not follow ground north out of the basin.

Descent reverses everything: back through the notch, down the north-east gully, then the wide south gully to camp.
hazards: The commonly published approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Alder, brush and wetland openings in the lower basin
Two gullies handed off to each other with a notch between; the transition at about 6,800 ft is the routefinding crux
Snow patches persist near the summit well into the season
Extremely remote from any US trailhead; the crest-trail approach is a multi-day walk each way

wa_castle_peak_pasayten_the_drawbridge._why: One of at least four lines on a fourteen-hundred-foot wall, and the only thing that separates it from its neighbours at the bottom is where the summit sits relative to your belay.
_sources: Route row's own approach, beta, descent_text and pitch_detail; the route's own published first-ascent report placing it on the central north buttress directly below the summit and noting at least four other routes on the face

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September, once the approach glacier and moraine are passable
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach that stays inside the United States, and it is a multi-day trudge rather than a walk.

From the highway pullout above the dam a short spur trail drops to the lake shore. Cross by water taxi or by a boat you portage down that spur, and land near the head of the lake where the Lightning Creek trail begins. Follow it, then pick up the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail, whose worst navigation is the steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the junction — intermittent orange flagging marks it. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a good waypoint and an emergency shelter; tread mostly dies around 4,200 ft.

The lower corridor is national recreation area and camping there needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, cross round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall. The glacier itself is mellow and allows easy travel.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The north face is a wall of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs about fourteen hundred feet high, holding ice or the remnants of it, with a glacier at its foot. It carries several routes and they are not marked, so identification is by POSITION AGAINST THE SUMMIT and nothing else.

THE TEST IS SIMPLE AND IT IS THE WHOLE IDENTIFICATION: this route takes the CENTRAL BUTTRESS, and that buttress sits DIRECTLY BELOW THE SUMMIT. Stand back on the glacier, find the summit on the skyline, and drop a plumb line from it. The buttress under that line is this route. If the summit is off to one side from where you are standing, you are under a different climb.

Getting onto it is the second problem. Expect an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock, and start with easy fifth-class ground whose purpose is to get out of the ROCKFALL LINE rather than to climb anything — that first pitch is a position move, not a feature.

CONFIRM ON PITCH TWO, because it arrives fast and it is unmistakable: the crux comes almost immediately, mid-fifth-class face climbing hard enough that the first ascent used a short aid move to pass it. A wall this size whose hardest pitch is the second one is unusual, and it is the strongest evidence you are on line.

The middle of the route then traverses out of a dihedral on a tricky flake and takes a roof on the LEFT via cracks and stemming, over slabs that needed heavy cleaning of dirt and moss. After about five pitches the route gains the ridge proper and the rock quality improves markedly, with one short harder hand-and-fist crack. The final technical pitch picks its way around teetering blocks, and then moderate snow slopes run the last four hundred feet to the top.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if your line starts in a blocky set of face holds beside a gully or chimney at the LEFT EDGE of the buttress, you are on the neighbouring route at the buttress's left margin, and higher up it follows a distinctive yellow quartz dyke that this route does not touch.

Descent is not the climb reversed. Walk off the south side and the east ridge back toward camp.
hazards: Several unmarked routes on one fourteen-hundred-foot wall; position under the summit is the only identifier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the start of the climbing
Rockfall on the lower wall; the first pitch exists mainly to escape the fall line
Dirt and moss-filled cracks through the middle section and teetering blocks near the top
Multi-day approach with no cell coverage and an extremely slow retreat

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE LEGAL POINT FIRST. This line walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and then crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it requires prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded here because it is the line the first ascent used and it is what most written accounts describe, not because it is a recommendation.

As described, it starts from the lake in the provincial park, climbs up and over Frosty Mountain, descends into the next creek basin to the south, traverses to the divide, and drops into the Crow Creek drainage below the peak's north face. The first ascent camped on the only dry spot on the ridge, roughly two-thirds of the way down toward the glacier.

The wholly lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
However you reach it, the glacier at the foot of the wall is the same and the identification is the same.

Come down the ridge from camp to the glacier, which is mellow enough to walk. Then stand back far enough to see the whole face at once — this is the step the approach itself makes easy from this side, because you descend toward the wall rather than arriving under it, and a descending approach gives you the one view that settles the route.

FROM THAT VIEW, DROP A PLUMB LINE FROM THE SUMMIT. The buttress under it is this route. The face carries several other lines and none is marked; being under the summit is the identification.

Watch for an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock. The first pitch is easy fifth-class ground taken to escape the ROCKFALL LINE rather than for the climbing, and the crux arrives at once on pitch two — face climbing hard enough that a short aid move was used on the first ascent.

NEGATIVE MARKER: a start in blocky face holds beside a gully or chimney at the LEFT EDGE of the buttress is the neighbouring route, which follows a yellow quartz dyke higher up.

Second negative marker, and it applies from the moment you leave camp: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line on this ground and it is not a route. The summit sits about a mile south of it.

Descent is the south side and the east ridge, unroped third and fourth-class ground from the top of the technical climbing, back toward camp.
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and two drainage divides with one dry camp on the ridge
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Rockfall on the lower face
Retreat from anywhere on this trip is measured in days

wa_north_face_left_buttress._why: Named for a side of a mountain that carries at least four routes, on the margin of the same buttress its neighbour climbs directly; without a feature test a party ties in under the wrong line.
_sources: Route row's own approach, beta, descent_text and pitch_detail naming the blocky face holds left of the gully or chimney on the left edge of the buttress and the yellow quartz dyke higher up; independent area summary confirming several lines on the face and both approaches

approach_variants.name: Ross Lake boat crossing, Lightning Creek and the abandoned Freezeout Creek trail to the north-face glacier
approach_variants.season: Summer; the documented ascent was made in early August
approach_variants.notes:
The approach that stays inside the United States, and much the longer of the two.

From the highway pullout above the dam, a spur trail drops to the lake shore; cross by water taxi or by a boat portaged down it, and land near the head of the lake. Follow the Lightning Creek trail, then the abandoned and increasingly brushy Freezeout Creek trail. The steep rock-and-alder diagonal immediately above the trail junction is the hardest navigation on the whole walk; look for intermittent orange flagging. The cabin at about 3,600 ft is a waypoint and an emergency shelter, and tread mostly disappears around 4,200 ft.

Camping in the lower corridor needs a park backcountry permit; the upper part is wilderness with a free self-issue permit.

From the upper basin, work round to the north side and onto the glacier at the foot of the wall, which is mellow enough for easy travel.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is about fourteen hundred feet of granite ribs, gullies and couloirs above a glacier and it carries several routes with nothing marked. Do not identify by name; identify by feature.

FIRST, PLACE THE CENTRAL BUTTRESS. Stand back on the glacier and find the summit, then look at the buttress directly beneath it — that is the neighbouring route, and this line is NOT on it. This route takes the LEFT MARGIN of that buttress system, so you want to be off to the left of the plumb line from the summit.

SECOND, FIND THE GULLY OR CHIMNEY AT THE BUTTRESS'S LEFT EDGE. The start is in the BLOCKY LINE OF FACE HOLDS JUST LEFT OF IT. Blocky face holds, immediately left of a gully or chimney, at the left edge of the buttress: that is the whole identification at the ground. The first pitch is long, mostly low fifth class, with a wide crack near its end.

THIRD, AND THIS IS THE CONFIRMATION HIGHER UP THAT NOTHING ELSE ON THE FACE GIVES YOU: this route follows a DISTINCTIVE YELLOW QUARTZ DYKE up the wall to avoid the dirtier rock either side of it. A yellow band running up the granite is not a subtle feature. If you never meet one, you are on a different climb.

Watch for an awkward BERGSCHRUND OR MOAT where the glacier meets the rock.

NEGATIVE MARKERS, and they matter because two of the neighbours are hard: if the summit is directly overhead from your belay and your second pitch is desperate face climbing wanting an aid move, you are on the central buttress line. And the face's original route and at least two others also exist here, so the honest rule is that anything without the yellow dyke above it is not this.

Descent is not the route reversed and not a rappel: take the east ridge from the top to an obvious col, then a snow finger back down toward the approach glacier and basin.
hazards: At least four unmarked lines on one wall, two of them starting close together on the same buttress
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the climbing
Roughly half the pitches are at the upper end of the grade, with the crux on a corner low down
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger, not by reversing the climb
Multi-day approach and a retreat measured in days

approach_variants.name: Provincial park approach from the north over Frosty Mountain to Crow Creek
approach_variants.season: Summer, once the divide traverse is clear enough to travel
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE LEGAL POINT FIRST. This approach walks in from the provincial park on the northern side and crosses the international boundary cross-country. That is not a lawful crossing. Away from a port of entry it needs prior arrangement with the border authority, the corridor is patrolled, and casual parties cannot simply walk over. It is recorded because it is the commonly published line and the shorter of the two, not as a recommendation.

As described, it takes the old trail along the creek to the boundary, then leaves the trail and travels cross-country south past Frosty Mountain, descending through the next creek basin and over the divide into the drainage below the peak's north face, finishing at the toe of the glacier.

The lawful alternatives are the boat crossing and abandoned creek trail from the east, or the crest trail from the west, both of which are considerably longer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whichever way you arrive, the glacier is the same and so is the identification, and this side has one advantage worth using: you come DOWN toward the wall, which gives you the whole face in one view before you are under it. Take that view rather than sorting the routes out from the bergschrund.

From back on the glacier, find the summit and note the buttress directly under it — that is the neighbouring line and it is not this one. This route is on the LEFT MARGIN of the same buttress system.

The ground marker is a GULLY OR CHIMNEY at the buttress's left edge, with the route starting in the BLOCKY LINE OF FACE HOLDS JUST LEFT OF IT. The confirmation above is a YELLOW QUARTZ DYKE, which the line follows deliberately to stay on clean rock and away from the dirtier granite either side. Yellow band, left margin, blocky start beside a chimney: those three together are the route.

Expect an awkward bergschrund or moat at the transition from ice to rock.

NEGATIVE MARKERS. Directly under the summit with a very hard second pitch means the central buttress line. No yellow dyke anywhere above you means one of the other lines on this face, of which there are several and none is marked.

Second negative marker and it is not about climbing: the boundary clearing is a visible cut line across this ground. It is not a route and it is not a shortcut.

Descent is the east ridge to an obvious col and then a snow finger back to the glacier and basin.
hazards: The described approach crosses the international boundary cross-country and is not a lawful crossing
Cross-country travel over a mountain and a drainage divide to reach the glacier
Awkward bergschrund or moat at the base of the wall
Several unmarked routes on one face, two of them on the same buttress
Descent by the east ridge and a snow finger rather than the way you came up

wa_west_ridge_2._why: One of two routes on a pinnacle inside a cluster of spires that all share one climbers' trail and one col; the two lines are reached by leaving that trail at different heights and neither leaves it at a marked point.
_sources: Route row's own approach, beta, descent_text and pitch_detail; independent trip accounts describing the contour right off the trail at the bench toward Paisano's lower section, the spring in the dry sandy gully, and a chockstone marking the start of the West Ridge

approach_variants.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib to the bench, then the contour right
approach_variants.season: Roughly June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access disappears when the highway closes
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain above rather than for the spires, and nothing marks the climbers' path.

The path drops down the talus and into the forest, crosses Early Winters Creek on a log, and then climbs steeply up the timbered rib on the LEFT — the north side — of the creek that drains the col above. Two hours or so of steep walking puts you on the basin bench at about 6,500 ft. There is a spring near the bench camp and it is the last reliable water.

From the bench the trail continues another three-quarters of an hour to the col at about 7,720 ft, which is the hub for the whole cluster. This route does not need to go that far.

The pullout doubles as the overnight for most parties. Nothing there is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE STARTS LOWER THAN EVERYTHING ELSE IN THE CLUSTER, and that is the fact to hold onto. The spires above the col get climbed from the col; this one does not.

Leave the col trail at the BENCH, around 6,600 ft, and CONTOUR RIGHT — south — around the bench toward the pinnacle's lower section. You are aiming for the toe of the ridge rather than for anything above you. There is a DRY SANDY GULLY on this contour with a SPRING in it, which is a useful confirmation that you are on the right ground and the last water before the climb.

The start itself is marked by a CHOCKSTONE — a jammed block at the foot of the ridge. That chockstone is the identification, and it is the reason accounts of this route keep saying to pay attention to the topo: without it, the lower ridge offers several plausible ways on and parties have burned an hour sorting it out.

If you come at it from the col instead, drop about two hundred feet of mostly fourth-class rock to sandy ledges just left of the pinnacle's top and work down and along; that reaches the same ground from above.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB. Seven or eight pitches of sustained mid-fifth-class hand and finger cracks along the ridge crest, with big comfortable belay ledges. The technical crux is about two-thirds of the way up on a short section of steep TWIN FINGER CRACKS. The last pitch is exposed, runout face climbing that most parties call the real crux for reasons that have nothing to do with the grade.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if you walked all the way to the col, then dropped a few hundred feet along the pinnacle's flank onto a third-class LEDGE SYSTEM and walked it rightward to a steep clean corner, you are at the other route on this pinnacle, several number grades harder. A ledge system leading to a corner is not this climb; a chockstone at the toe of a ridge is.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER: the neighbouring spire's north face is the usual link-up partner and its routes start from the col itself. Being at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are at this route.

Descent is a few hundred feet of downclimbing, then two rappels of about thirty and twenty metres into the gully beneath the col, downclimbing between the anchors, then the trail back past the bench.
hazards: Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path with no trail signs anywhere
The start is a single jammed block; the lower ridge offers several plausible wrong starts
The final pitch is runout exposed face climbing with marginal protection
Rope drag on the long crest pitch if slings are not managed
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water

wa_rampage._why: Reached by leaving the shared col trail across a loose slope onto a ledge system, then walking that ledge to its far end; every part of that is unmarked and its neighbour on the same pinnacle starts hundreds of feet lower.
_sources: Route row's own approach, beta, descent_text and pitch_detail; independent accounts describing the cut right across a loose slope to the left end of an obvious ledge system, following it right to the base of the corner, and reaching it by descending about 300 ft from the col

approach_variants.name: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib, then the ledge system below the col
approach_variants.season: Roughly late June through September; the approach holds snow into June and access ends with the highway closure
approach_variants.notes:
Park in the broad unsigned pullout on the highway about four miles east of Washington Pass, at roughly 4,250 to 4,300 ft. It is signed for the mountain rather than for the spires, and the climbers' path itself is unmarked.

Go down the talus and into the forest, cross Early Winters Creek on a log, and climb the steep timbered rib on the LEFT, the north side, of the creek draining the col. About two hours brings you to the basin bench at roughly 6,500 ft, where there is a spring — the last reliable water.

From the bench another three-quarters of an hour or so gains the col at about 7,720 ft. Unlike its neighbour on the same pinnacle, this route wants you high, so keep going up.

The pullout is where most parties sleep. It is undeveloped and the highway is audible all night.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE IS REACHED FROM HIGH, NOT FROM LOW, and that single sentence separates it from the other line on this pinnacle.

There are two ways onto its ledge, described from opposite directions and they meet in the same place. Either cut RIGHT off the col trail before topping out, crossing a VERY LOOSE SLOPE to gain the LEFT END of an obvious LEDGE SYSTEM; or go all the way to the col and DESCEND ABOUT THREE HUNDRED FEET along the pinnacle's flank to the same ledge. Both are quick.

THEN WALK THE LEDGE RIGHTWARD TO ITS FAR END. This is the step people skip. The ledge is third class and it goes further than you expect; the route does not start where you step onto it. Keep going until the ledge runs out.

AT THE FAR RIGHT END OF THE LEDGE, A STEEP CLEAN CORNER RISES STRAIGHT OFF IT. That corner is the route. It is a big obvious corner system on the right side of the pinnacle's main face, and the climbing in it is continuous, clean and steep — the physical test is that the rock quality is conspicuously better than the loose slope you crossed to get there.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB. Pitch one is moderate with a chimney-behind-a-block move. Pitch two is the standout: a steep continuous corner to a TRIANGULAR ROOF, passed on finger locks. Pitch three is the hardest, off a DETACHED FLAKE into steep flaring finger and hand jams on the left wall. Pitch four is corner climbing into an offwidth section. A triangular roof on the second pitch and a detached flake on the third are the two features that settle it.

NEGATIVE MARKER: if you left the trail down at the BENCH around 6,600 ft, contoured right past a spring in a dry sandy gully, and found a CHOCKSTONE at the toe of a ridge, you are at the other route on this pinnacle — several number grades easier and a different day. A chockstone at a ridge toe is not this climb; a corner at the far right end of a ledge is.

SECOND NEGATIVE MARKER: the neighbouring spire's routes start from the col itself and are the usual link-up partner. Standing at the col with rock above you is not evidence you are here; you still have to lose height.

At the top, either scramble third-class ground north-east toward the neighbouring spire's north face to continue a link-up, downclimbing over precariously stacked blocks and flakes, or make two thirty-metre rappels down the gully back to the col.
hazards: A very loose slope is crossed to gain the approach ledge, above the col trail
The route starts at the far right end of the ledge, not where you step onto it
Precariously stacked blocks and flakes on the scramble toward the neighbouring spire
Unsigned pullout and unmarked climbers' path
Early Winters Creek is crossed on a log and is worse in high water

wa_playing_not_spraying._why: The row stores two different approaches to this formation and they serve opposite sides of it; the face this route is on is reached from the south, and there are two long routes on that face which share a summit.
_sources: Route row's own beta, descent_text and the trailhead waypoint note describing the valley trail and the creek draining the south side; independent area description giving the same south-side access and the meadow camp; sibling route row read against it

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-June through late September; July and August are the driest and most reliable
approach_variants.notes:
THE APPROACH THAT MATTERS HERE IS THE SOUTHERN ONE, AND IT IS NOT THE SPIRES TRAIL. The climbers' path from the unsigned pullout further west serves the spires and the col on the other side of the crest. It does not put you under this face.

For the south face, walk the Cedar Creek trail from its own trailhead off the highway. After roughly five miles, turn off to the RIGHT below the old burn, where a rough path follows the RIGHT-HAND side of the creek that drains the south side of the formation.

There are good meadows for camping at about 6,200 ft. This is a rarely visited corner and there is no established climbers' camp, no fixed gear on the approach and very little traffic — expect to see nobody.

A parking pass or day fee covers the trailhead. This is national forest, so there is no permit system and no quota, and the general dispersed-camping rules apply.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The face is CLEAN WHITE GRANITE, which is the first confirmation and a good one — it is visibly paler than the rock either side and it is why the formation gets climbed at all. Follow the creek up to the meadows and then to the foot of that white wall. Two long routes share it and they share a summit, so the identification has to be done at the ground and re-checked on the climb.

THE START IS A FLAKE, AND IT IS A BIG ONE. This route begins with a LAYBACK OFF A LARGE CLEAN FLAKE that leads into a LONG LEFT-FACING CORNER SYSTEM carrying finger cracks. Large detached flake at the bottom, left-facing corner above it: that pairing is the whole identification and there is nothing else on this face like it.

CONFIRM WITH THE ROOFS, IN ORDER. Above the corner system the route crosses RIGHT beneath a ROOF into a SPLITTER CRACK that reaches a ledge partway up the face. Higher, a SECOND ROOF leads to a hand crack and then stemming corners with a hard exit. Two roofs, the first crossed rightward and the second climbed through, is the sequence.

THE SUMMIT PITCH IS THE CLEANEST TEST OF ALL, and it is worth knowing before you leave the ledge: this route tops out THROUGH A DEEP SUMMIT CHIMNEY. You finish inside the chimney. The other long route on this face finishes on blocky ground JUST RIGHT OF that chimney and never enters it. If you are stemming a deep slot to the top, you are on this route; if you are scrambling blocks beside one, you are on the neighbour.

NEGATIVE MARKER at the start to match it: if you began on the RIGHT-HAND side of the face on flakes, corners and splitters and arrived at a BROAD LEDGE running most of the way across the face at about half height, you are on the neighbouring line. This route has no such crossing ledge low down; its mid-height ledge is reached from a splitter after a rightward move under a roof.

Protection throughout is cams and nuts to about three inches. Descent is a series of rappels down the south-east side; a seventy-metre rope is the standard, fixed anchors are sparse, and you should expect to build some — carry extra webbing.
hazards: The row's own stored approach describes the spires trail on the far side of the crest; use the southern valley approach for this face
Rarely climbed, so there is no traffic, no chalk and essentially no current conditions information
Rappel anchors on the descent are sparse and some must be built; carry extra webbing
Two long routes share this face and its summit
Remote enough that a retreat from high on the face is slow

wa_the_chalice._why: Shares a face, a summit and a mid-face ledge with its neighbour; the row also carries two conflicting approaches, only one of which reaches this side of the formation.
_sources: Route row's own beta and the trailhead waypoint note describing the valley trail and the creek draining the south side; independent area description giving the same south-side access, the turn below the burn and the meadow camp; sibling route row read against it

approach_variants.name: Cedar Creek trail from the highway, then the creek draining the south side
approach_variants.season: Roughly mid-June through late September; July and August are typically driest
approach_variants.notes:
THE SPIRES TRAIL IS THE WRONG APPROACH FOR THIS FACE. The unsigned pullout further west and the col above it serve the spires on the other side of the crest, not the southern wall this route is on.

Take the Cedar Creek trail from its own trailhead off the highway. At roughly five miles, turn off to the RIGHT below the old burn; a rough path then follows the RIGHT-HAND side of the creek draining the south side of the formation. Meadows at about 6,200 ft give good camping.

This is a quiet corner by the standards of this highway. There is no established climbers' camp, no fixed approach gear and effectively no traffic.

A parking pass or day fee covers the trailhead; there is no permit system and no quota on national forest ground here.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The wall is CLEAN WHITE GRANITE and it is visibly paler than what surrounds it, which is the first check that you are under the right formation. Follow the creek to the meadows and then up to the foot of it.

THIS ROUTE IS THE RIGHT-HAND LINE. Start on the RIGHT SIDE of the south face, on flakes, corners and splitters. Its neighbour begins with a layback off a LARGE CLEAN FLAKE into a long LEFT-FACING corner system; if that is what is above you, walk right.

THE DEFINING FEATURE IS A BROAD LEDGE AT HALF HEIGHT, and it is the strongest thing this route has. Roughly halfway up the face the climbing arrives at a wide ledge that runs across the wall. That ledge is the route's hinge: from it you WALK LEFTWARD before starting the upper half. A route that reaches a broad crossing ledge and then requires you to walk left along it is this one.

CONFIRM ON THE UPPER FACE. The first pitch above the ledge heads for the LEFT SIDE OF THE MOST PROMINENT ARETE OR PILLAR in the middle of the upper wall. That arete is the biggest feature up there and being on its left is the check. Two more pitches, then the line trends RIGHTWARD to the summit.

THE SUMMIT PITCH SEPARATES THE TWO ROUTES ABSOLUTELY. This one finishes on BLOCKY GROUND JUST RIGHT OF A PROMINENT CHIMNEY. It does not go into the chimney. The neighbouring route tops out THROUGH a deep summit chimney. So: blocky ground beside a slot means this route; stemming up inside the slot means you have crossed onto the other line.

NEGATIVE MARKER lower down, since the two lines are close: if there was no broad crossing ledge and instead you moved rightward under a roof into a splitter to reach a smaller ledge, you are on the neighbour.

Descent is not separately documented for this line. Because it shares the summit and the mid-face ledge with its neighbour, parties use that route's rappels down the south-east side: a seventy-metre rope, sparse fixed anchors, and enough webbing to build your own. Treat that as an inference rather than a described descent and go up prepared to make anchors.

Its own descent is not separately documented; the shared rappel line is an inference from the shared summit
Rappel anchors are sparse and some must be built; carry extra webbing
Rarely climbed, so there is no chalk, no traffic and no current conditions information
Two long routes on one face that share a mid-height ledge and a summit
